newsitem.title: USA: CIA says lone analyst made Gulf war gas link.
newsitem.headline: CIA says lone analyst made Gulf war gas link.

text.p: CIA officials say a five-year delay in confirming possible Gulf War troops' exposure to war gas was not a cover-up, and that they simply did not see the connection until last year when an analyst heard a radio interview.

CIA officials said at a Senate hearing this week that analyst Larry Fox made the connection last March 10, when he heard a Gulf War veteran describe in a radio interview how U.S. troops blew up an Iraqi weapons dump after the 1991 war and realised it was the same depot the CIA by then believed had contained war gas weapons.

The CIA officials said they contacted the Defence Department the next day and that further investigation led to Pentagon announcements last summer that the weapons dump explosions may have exposed up to 20,000 U.S. troops to low levels of war gas.

But Senate Veterans Affairs Committee Chairman Arlen Specter was not satisfied. He said that the committee will investigate whether the Defence Department tried to cover up the possible gas war exposure or was simply indifferent to it.
"That we are going to pursue in depth," Specter, a Pennsylvania Republican, said at the Senate hearing.

The Pentagon has already acknowledged that Iraqis told U.N. inspectors in 1991 the ammunition dump at Kamisiyah in southern Iraq had contained chemical war weapons and that that report was passed on to the CIA and the Pentagon.

But it said the report got lost until President Bill Clinton ordered U.S. government agencies to review all Gulf War records that might explain why thousands of U.S. troops returned home from the war sick.
"Nobody realised the significance of the (1991) memo at the time," a defence official said on Friday.

Nearly 700,000 U.S. troops served in the 1991 war to drive Iraqi forces out of Kuwait. Federal studies have concluded after examination of 80,000 of them that there is no single Gulf War syndrome, but federal doctors have been unable to diagnose at least 5,000 of the veterans' illnesses.

Acting CIA Director George Tenet and two other CIA officials told Specter's committee that the 1991 report of possible chemical weapons at Kamisiyah was lost partly because both U.N. and U.S. officials were suspicious at the time that Iraq was trying to mislead them.

But they said that after Clinton ordered all agencies to review their records, the CIA concluded in September 1995 that there were three sites in Iraq where low levels of war gas could have been released, and the most likely was Kamisiyah.

By early March last year, they said, CIA and Pentagon analysts established that U.S. troops may have blown up part of the Iraqi weapons dump. That was confirmed on March 10 when CIA analyst Fox listened at home to a tape recording of a Baltimore talk show in which Gulf War veteran Brian Martin described how U.S. troops blew up the dump, and further investigation proved it.
